content.text:
Check this scene against the index and the scene card.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an
index *before* this scene is folded in. index-manager writes them at commit, from this
prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns
nothing for these two` are not findings; they are what a first appearance looks like.

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference. Breaking a genre promise deliberately is legitimate; it has to be visibly deliberate.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

Verify s-001 for P1 consistency, mechanical plausibility, and craft. Pay special attention to: locked-room claims (door locked from inside, windows latched, no weapon), the stopped watch time (obj-pocket-watch) and whether quoting object provenance lines is allowed as done, the use of the mantel clock as an audial timing device (recall-mantel-chime-pattern), and any implicit claims about Alfred's appearance or hands (this was a staged behavioural cue — allowed as writer's choice). Flag any missing provenance, contradictions with world_rules, or craft issues such as 'telling not showing' or too many stage-direction inventions. Return the audit file path and verdict.

That is in addition to your standing instructions above, not instead of them.
If it states a story fact that is not in your packet — a name, a measurement, a
quotation, a piece of history — that fact has not been checked against the index by
anyone. Ask about it or establish it yourself in the state delta. Do not write it down
as though it were already true.

# Context packet — scene s-001

## P0

### scene-card  <novel/chapters/ch-01/chapter.yaml>

Scene s-001. Intent: Open the case: establish narrator, setting and stakes; present the locked-room puzzle and immediate physical constraints (locked door, latched windows, no weapon). Show the assembled cast and their motives; plant the first physical clues — stopped pocket watch, worn spot on obj-chair-study, and the mantel clock's chime as a timing device.
Present: char-james-cole, char-victor-hale, char-lucy-hale, char-alfred-broome, char-owen-myers, char-evelyn-ross, loc-hale-mansion, loc-study, loc-foyer, obj-chair-study, obj-mantel-clock, obj-pocket-watch, obj-will-draft
Target length: about 700 words.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

A private detective is called to a provincial manor where a clock‑obsessed collector is found stabbed in a study locked from the inside; with suspects trapped by circumstance and a corpse bearing a single, inexplicable wound, the detective must untangle mechanical cunning from human motive before the murderer can cover the last, smallest clue.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-james-cole: Narrator and private detective in his mid-40s. Methodical, world-weary, sceptical; tells the story in first person.
- char-victor-hale: Victim: a sixty-year-old collector of automatons and clocks, proprietorial and sharp-tongued. Killed in his locked study.
- char-lucy-hale: Victor's niece and heir-presumptive: practical, plainspoken, lives in the house. Financial motive if Victor changes his will.
- char-alfred-broome: The butler: stoic, old-school, formerly a railway machinist. Knows his way around springs and clockwork. Long service to the Hales.
- char-owen-myers: Local clock repairman and collector acquaintance of Victor. Skilled with small mechanisms, sometimes quarrels with Victor over valuations.
- char-evelyn-ross: Rival collector and a guest that evening: charming, ruthless in business, interested in acquiring Victor's most prized automaton.
- char-dr-simms: Local coroner. Clinical, precise; provides the autopsy details that constrain the timeline.
- loc-hale-mansion: Victorian manor on the outskirts of a market town. Has a family study where the murder takes place.
- loc-study: Victor's private study: heavy oak furniture, tall bookcases, a single inward-opening door with an old lock, and a high mantelpiece with a mantel clock. Windows are latched from the inside.
- loc-foyer: Entrance hall where guests are received and where the household gathers after the body is found.
- loc-kitchen: Service wing where Alfred and staff work; Alfred claims to have been here around the time of death.
- obj-chair-study: Victor's heavy upholstered study chair — the site where he was found slumped. It bears old repairs and a faint circular wear spot on the left rear seam.
- obj-mantel-clock: A gilt 19th-century mantel clock on the study mantelpiece. Chimes every quarter-hour. Victor prized its inner mechanism.
- obj-pocket-watch: Victor's gold pocket watch found stopped on his person; the minute hand bent and the watch stopped at a time relevant to establishing the minute of death.
- obj-spring-spike-device: A concealed, spring-loaded stiletto-like spike — the hypothesised mechanism that could deliver a single, retracting wound and leave no conventional weapon in the room.
- obj-rail-ticket: A train ticket in Owen Myers's possession; the ticket is his claimed alibi for leaving town that night.
- obj-file-rasp: A small metal rasp with fresh filings in its teeth; could link a person to work on tiny metal parts.
- obj-will-draft: A draft copy of Victor's new will, suggesting he intended to cut someone out; its existence supplies motive.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- No supernatural explanations: every effect must have a physical, human-scale cause.
- All mechanical trickery and forensics must be physically plausible with late-19th/early-20th-century to contemporary hand tools and clockwork; no exotic or high-tech gadgets.
- Locked-room means the study's door is locked from the inside and windows are latched; there are no unknown or unexplored secret passages unless explicitly named as an entity in the plan.
- Detective's methods are limited to human observation, conversation, reconstruction, and standard local forensic input (char-dr-simms); no omniscient leaps or unavailable lab results.
- Every clue introduced in a scene must have a discoverable physical source (an object, a mark, a document, or a witness) present in the plan's entity list.

## The draft

I arrived at Hale Mansion close to nine and found a party that had been turned polite and small by a corpse. The house kept its old shape — steep roof, stone steps, a lantern guttering at the porch — and inside the air smelled of tea gone cold and varnish. I tell you this because detail is the only thing that steadies you in a room where someone has just stopped being anything at all.

Victor Hale lay in his study as if his last conversation had been with the fabric of his own chair. He was slumped in the heavy upholstered seat by the mantel, the chair itself looking as if it had held him for decades: "Victor's heavy upholstered study chair — the site where he was found slumped. It bears old repairs and a faint circular wear spot on the left rear seam." That line is not mine; it is the chair. It was where he had stopped.

The study's door was locked from the inside, and every window in that room was latched. I saw the latch on the high window and a hand had banged the lock closed. The household had not forced anything; the scene was intact in the way a watch is intact when it simply will not run. There was, on inspection, no conventional weapon in the room. Whoever had done this had left no knife on the carpet, no blunt instrument on the desk: only the body and its last arrangements.

On his person lay his watch — gold, small, ruined in one graceful way: "Victor's gold pocket watch found stopped on his person; the minute hand bent and the watch stopped at a time relevant to establishing the minute of death." The watch had indeed stopped. The minute hand had been bent; the watch read 9:14 p.m. I note the time because I have to. The mantel clock, which had been Victor's pride, gave me the measure of the house: "The mantel clock, a gilt 19th-century piece, chimes every quarter-hour; its mechanism was Victor's pride." It chimes in the old pattern — one at the quarter, two at the half, three at the three-quarters, four on the hour — and in the hall the chime had already marked the evening for us once.

In the foyer the household and the night's guests had been gathered. Lucy Hale stood by the newel, hands clasped so tight the knuckles showed white; she was plainspoken in her grief and in her fear — inheritance anxiety, you could call it, though that is a small thing when a man is dead. Alfred Broome, the butler, kept his face nearly blank; the stoic, old-school air of a man who has spent his life managing other people's exactness. I had the sense — and I say this as a writer's choice of what to stage, not as evidence yet in someone's testimony — that Alfred's fingers were oil-stained, that the old railway machinist had the calm of someone familiar with springs and clockwork.

Owen Myers hovered, aggrieved and quick to snap a remark; he is a clock repairman and collector, skilled with small mechanisms and apt to quarrel with Victor over the worth of a thing. Evelyn Ross smiled with the thin courtesy of business; she was the collector who wanted what Victor kept, every polite syllable counting toward acquisition. Between them the motive map was plain: the draft of a new will had been found on Victor's desk and it suggested he intended to cut someone out — "A draft copy of Victor's new will, suggesting he intended to cut someone out; its existence supplies motive." That document sat in the study like a promise and a threat both.

The study itself offered a handful of physical cues that I filed in the order my hands could reach them: a faint abrasion at the chair frame, dust pressed and tufted where someone had shifted, a bent minute hand on a dead watch that read 9:14, and the worn, circular spot on the left rear seam of the chair where a pocket or a shoulder might have rubbed for years. The mantel clock's mechanism — Victor's pride — would be the measure by which we might place a minute to a sound.

A locked door, latched windows, a stopped watch, a worn patch on a chair, a draft will and a company of people with reasons to want a change. That is what the house offered me when it opened its door. I stood in the foyer, the mantle chiming, and promised myself I would make the room speak.

arguments.quote: The study itself offered a handful of physical cues that I filed in the order my hands could reach them: a faint abrasion at the chair frame, dust pressed and tufted where someone had shifted, a bent minute hand on a dead watch that read 9:14, and the worn, circular spot on the left rear seam of the chair where a pocket or a shoulder might have rubbed for years.
arguments.reasoning: The paragraph lists the scene's physical clues as a summary rather than dramatising their discovery. The scene's purpose is to plant these clues vividly; presenting them as an inventory reduces immediacy and misses an opportunity to show the detective's methodical inspection, which is central to establishing tone and procedure.
arguments.suggestion: Turn this inventory into a short sequence of beats. For example: have the narrator bend to the chair, fingers find the worn seam, pause at the abrasion, lift the watch to his palm and feel its cold face, notice (and describe) the bent minute hand as a physical sensation, then look up to the mantel as a chime begins. Replace the comma-separated list with two or three short, concrete sentences that dramatise touching, smelling, and hearing—so the clues are discovered in time and the reader experiences the detective's method.
arguments.state_after: The scene currently names the clues but does not dramatise their discovery; after the fix the same clues should be introduced through a short physical inspection sequence.
arguments.state_before: The clues are presented as a summarized list of items the narrator 'filed' mentally.

arguments.quote: "Victor's heavy upholstered study chair — the site where he was found slumped. It bears old repairs and a faint circular wear spot on the left rear seam." That line is not mine; it is the chair. It was where he had stopped.
arguments.reasoning: Dropping verbatim provenance lines into the narrator's first-person voice and following them with a meta-comment ('That line is not mine; it is the chair') breaks the voice and reads like stage direction or an index dump. It interrupts immersion and reduces the detective's observational authority. The scene is stronger if the provenance phrasing is integrated into the narrator's sensory impressions rather than quoted as an external citation.
arguments.suggestion: Remove the literal provenance quote and fold its details into the narrator's voice. For example: 'The chair—heavy, upholstered, stitched and re-stitched—held him as if it had been expecting him; a faint circular wear spot marked the left rear seam.' Delete the meta-comment 'That line is not mine; it is the chair.' If you want an echo of the object's registered description, distill it into one short, ironic aside in the narrator's tone rather than a verbatim quote.
arguments.state_before: The scene inserts verbatim object-file lines into narration and follows with a meta-comment ('That line is not mine; it is the chair.'), creating a tonal jolt.
arguments.state_after: The same factual content (old repairs; faint circular wear spot) is present but expressed as part of the narrator's sensory observation, restoring voice continuity and immersion.

arguments.quote: I tell you this because detail is the only thing that steadies you in a room where someone has just stopped being anything at all.
arguments.reasoning: This sentence explicitly states the scene's thematic claim ('detail steadies you') rather than letting the detective's method and the scene's micro-observations embody it. It reads like an authorial thesis line and risks reducing the scene's emotional resonance by telling the reader what to take away instead of showing it through the investigation.
arguments.suggestion: Either remove or soften the line and let the narrator's inspection demonstrate the idea. For example, cut it or replace with a short, concrete sentence that shows the effect: 'I reach for the chair's seam because habit tells me that's where a life leaves its rub.' Keep the thematic point implicit in the detective's actions and sensory notes.
arguments.state_before: Scene opens with an explicit thematic line asserting that 'detail steadies you.'
arguments.state_after: After the fix, the theme should be carried by the narrator's actions and precise sensory details rather than an explicit statement.

content.text:
Summary verdict
- Consistency: PASS. I found no consistency/factual defects to block the scene. The deterministic comparison already showed all claims in this draft are first establishments; nothing contradicts the index or world rules.
- Mechanical plausibility / locked-room checks: OK. The locked-door, latched-windows, no conventional weapon, stopped pocket watch (9:14), and mantel-chime-as-timer are all present and used within the allowed world-rules constraints. No impossible mechanic or undeclared gadget appears in the prose.
- Craft: THREE recorded craft warnings (see below). These are stylistic and pacing issues that the writer should fix before committing.

Audit file path and verdict
- Audit file: continuity/verifier/s-001-audit.json
- Verdict: Consistency cleared for P1; scene needs a single short repair round focused on dramatizing clue discovery and smoothing provenance-quote voice. After those craft edits, the scene is ready to commit.

What I recorded (one craft finding per recorded defect)
1) summary_not_scene (warning)
- Quote (offending passage): "The study itself offered a handful of physical cues that I filed in the order my hands could reach them: a faint abrasion at the chair frame, dust pressed and tufted where someone had shifted, a bent minute hand on a dead watch that read 9:14, and the worn, circular spot on the left rear seam of the chair where a pocket or a shoulder might have rubbed for years."
- Why: The paragraph inventories the clues rather than dramatizing their discovery. The scene's job is to plant these clues vividly and to show the detective's method; listing them as an index reduces immediacy and flattens the opening beat.
- Suggestion: Replace the list with a short sequence of inspection beats (touch the seam, lift the watch, feel its cold face, note the bent minute hand, pause at the abrasion as the mantel begins to chime), so the reader experiences discovery in time with the detective.
- State before / after: before — clues are presented as a summarised inventory; after — same clues introduced through physical beats and sensory detail.

2) flat_diction / provenance-quote usage (warning)
- Quote (offending passage): "\"Victor's heavy upholstered study chair — the site where he was found slumped. It bears old repairs and a faint circular wear spot on the left rear seam.\" That line is not mine; it is the chair. It was where he had stopped."
- Why: Dropping verbatim provenance lines into the first-person voice and then stepping out with a meta-comment ("That line is not mine; it is the chair.") breaks narrative immersion and reads like stage direction. The packet explicitly provides provenance phrasing (see recall-provenance-quotes in the scene packet), so quoting is allowed — but it should be integrated, not quoted as an index entry.
- Suggestion: Remove the verbatim quote and fold the facts into the narrator's sensory phrasing (e.g., "The chair—stitched and re-stitched—held him as if expecting him; a faint circular wear spot puckered the left rear seam."). If you want an echo of the registered description, make it a brief, in-character aside in the narrator's voice rather than an external citation.

3) theme_stated (warning)
- Quote (offending passage): "I tell you this because detail is the only thing that steadies you in a room where someone has just stopped being anything at all."
- Why: This explicit statement of theme tells rather than shows. The scene will be stronger if the detective's actions and precise observations embody this idea.
- Suggestion: Cut or soften the sentence and show the theme through action. Example replacement: "I reach for the chair's seam; habit and a lifetime of looking tell me where a life leaves its rub." Let the investigation demonstrate the steadiness detail provides.

Notes on the special checks called out in the brief
- Quoting provenance lines: permitted. The packet explicitly provided verbatim provenance lines (recall-provenance-quotes / objects/* files). Using them is allowed, but as above, integrate rather than dump them into the narrator's voice.
- Mantel clock as timing device: correctly used. The draft uses the quarter-hour chime pattern provided in the packet and links it to measurement; that usage aligns with recall-mantel-chime-pattern and recall-mantel-use-note.
- Stopped pocket watch time (obj-pocket-watch = 9:14): established by the scene and consistent with the packet's obj-pocket-watch description.
- Alfred's implied hands/finger marks: the draft frames the detail ("I had the sense... that Alfred's fingers were oil-stained") as a staged observation and explicitly flags it as the narrator's interpretive staging ("I say this as a writer's choice... not as evidence yet in someone's testimony"), which is acceptable. No consistency error.

What I did not report as defects (and why)
- No consistency finding for the direct quoting of object/object-file lines: the scene packet explicitly supplied those verbatim lines for use. The issue is craft (integration), not canon mismatch.
- No contradiction with world_rules about locked-room or absence of weapon: the scene asserts "no conventional weapon," which is consistent with the plan (the hypothesised spring-spike device exists in the plan but is a later hypothesis, not asserted here).
- No timeline contradiction: narrator arrives "close to nine" and the stopped watch reads 9:14; both can be true without contradiction (arrival time is approximate).

Recommended next step for the writer (concrete and actionable)
- Perform one short revision pass (about 2–5 paragraphs):
  1) Convert the inventory paragraph into a 3–4 beat inspection sequence (touch, lift, smell, listen) so discovery unfolds in time with the mantel chime.
  2) Remove or recast the verbatim object-file quote about the chair; fold those details into the narrator's voice.
  3) Replace or soften the explicit theme sentence so the detective's actions imply the theme.
With those three focused edits the scene will satisfy the scene card, keep the useful provenance language, and read with steadier voice and more immediacy.

- objects/obj-chair-study.yaml — exact provenance line supplied for the chair.
- objects/obj-pocket-watch.yaml — exact provenance line for the watch (stopped; bent minute hand).
- objects/obj-mantel-clock.yaml — chime pattern and usage notes.
(These were included in the scene packet as recall-provenance-quotes and may be used verbatim if integrated smoothly.)
